back: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.
Weak acid + its salt (e.g. CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa), or partly neutralise a weak acid with a strong base.
Added H⁺: A⁻ + H⁺ → HA. Added OH⁻: HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O. The ratio [HA]/[A⁻] changes little.
[H⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻]; pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Amounts may replace concentrations.
pH = pKa; a buffer works best within about 1 pH unit of its pKa.
H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ keeps blood at about pH 7.4; excess CO₂ is breathed out.
pOH = pKb + log([NH₄⁺]/[NH₃]); pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.
Buffers cope only with small additions; once one reservoir is used up, the pH changes sharply.
Humus acids, clay and carbonates buffer soil pH; lime is added when soils become too acidic.
